title: Comcast loses more customers, claims other ISPs' cheap prices are "irrational"
gist: Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026 (versus 91,000 a year earlier) and 274,000 video customers. Its management blamed fixed-wireless share gains and "irrational" $30-$40 fiber offers, which the CFO says cannot recoup fiber build costs of $1,500+ per home. Comcast is starting its largest-ever cost transformation, with a charge of over $1 billion in Q4, reported cable-division job cuts and more AI customer-service agents (Sierra, Cresta). The stock rose after the company beat overall earnings estimates even as connectivity revenue fell 2.6 percent.

insights.claim: Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000 loss in Q3 2025, leaving 28.3 million US residential broadband customers. Losses were larger than analysts expected.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Faster broadband losses undercut the main profit engine of cable; a negative read-through for Charter and other cable operators.
insights.locator: Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts

insights.claim: Comcast lost 274,000 video customers in Q3 2026, versus 257,000 a year earlier, bringing total video customers down to 10.4 million.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Cord-cutting continues to speed up, showing that pay-TV decline is structural.

insights.claim: Comcast's total broadband subscribers rose every quarter for 20 years until a net loss of 10,000 in Q2 2022. A Q1 2025 loss of 183,000 led co-CEO Mike Cavanagh to say the company was not "winning in the marketplace." Unlimited data and a five-year price guarantee starting at $45 a month have not stopped the losses.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Retention moves are not working, which points to structural share loss rather than a cyclical dip.

insights.claim: Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong says more customers are leaving at "pricing transitions," meaning when promotional rates expire. The company is refining offers and retention strategies to manage those moments.
insights.speaker: Jason Armstrong
insights.so_what: Price increases after promotions are now a churn trigger, which limits Comcast's pricing power on ARPU.

themes.theme: Competition from fiber and fixed wireless

insights.claim: Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh says fixed wireless remains aggressive and keeps taking share, while fiber construction stays elevated with "pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity."
insights.speaker: Mike Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Fixed-wireless providers and fiber builders are taking share from cable; this favors FWA carriers and fiber overbuilders.
insights.quote: Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity

insights.claim: Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong calls $30-$40 monthly fiber broadband offers "irrational" because fiber deployment costs $1,500 or more per home and is getting more expensive in suburban and rural areas. Verizon, which he did not name, has been pitching FiOS fiber plans starting at $30 a month.
insights.speaker: Jason Armstrong
insights.so_what: If Comcast is right, fiber overbuilders' returns are at risk; if not, cable faces lasting price pressure. Watch fiber operators' ARPU and build costs.
insights.quote: As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition

insights.claim: Comcast's network is a mix of fiber and cable, with fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its territory. Comcast historically benefited from little competition in high-speed wired broadband.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Comcast's former monopoly-like position is wearing away as fiber arrives in its markets.

insights.claim: Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh says satellite broadband is "not yet a material factor" in Comcast's competition, though the company is preparing for emerging forms of competition.
insights.speaker: Mike Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Satellite (e.g. LEO broadband) is a watch-list risk for cable but not yet in the numbers.
insights.quote: satellite is not yet a material factor

themes.theme: Cost transformation, job cuts and AI agents

insights.claim: Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh calls the company's new program the most significant operating and cost transformation in its history, an opportunity he believes will be worth billions of dollars over time. CFO Jason Armstrong says it will bring a charge of over $1 billion in Q4 2026.
insights.speaker: Mike Cavanagh
insights.so_what: Expect a Q4 restructuring charge of more than $1 billion and margin-expansion guidance; billions in savings is the bull case.
insights.quote: We’ve embarked on the most significant operating and cost transformation in our company’s history

insights.claim: Bloomberg and Variety report that Comcast plans significant job cuts in its cable, broadband and wireless businesses, not in NBCUniversal divisions. Comcast has not specified how many jobs will go.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Headcount reductions in the cable division support the cost-cut thesis.

insights.claim: Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong says AI is embedded across its network and is expanding into customer experience through partnerships with Sierra and Cresta. He says customer service contact rates are already down about 20 percent, with more than 30 million service interactions eliminated year to date.
insights.speaker: Jason Armstrong
insights.so_what: A real enterprise case of AI agents replacing call-center work, which validates vendors like Sierra and Cresta.
insights.quote: We’ve already reduced customer service contact rates by roughly 20 percent and eliminated more than 30 million service interactions year-to-date versus the prior year.

insights.claim: Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong says the company is positioning itself to benefit as personal AI agents change how consumers discover, buy and manage services.
insights.speaker: Jason Armstrong
insights.so_what: Telecoms are starting to plan around AI agents as a sales and service channel.
insights.quote: As personal AI agents reshape how consumers discover, purchase, and manage services, we’re positioning Comcast to capitalize on that shift

insights.claim: Comcast added 368,000 wireless lines in Q3 2026, down from 414,000 a year earlier and below analyst estimates. It now has 10.6 million lines.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Slowing wireless growth weakens the bundle as an offset to broadband losses.

insights.claim: Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong defends giving broadband customers a free wireless line for a year as rational, because Comcast is an MVNO reselling Verizon capacity with no spectrum or towers. He says about 70 percent of free lines convert to paying relationships at $30 a month, which requires a home Internet bundle.
insights.speaker: Jason Armstrong
insights.so_what: The capital-light MVNO bundle helps reduce broadband churn and brings Verizon wholesale revenue.
insights.quote: We don’t have spectrum. We don’t have towers. Our model is an MVNO [Mobile Virtual Network Operator] model.

insights.claim: Comcast's Q3 2026 revenue fell to $29.3 billion from $31.2 billion while net income rose to $3.45 billion from $3.33 billion. The stock rose after the company beat overall earnings expectations, helped by a profit from Peacock.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The market rewarded the earnings beat and Peacock's profit despite the subscriber miss, a sign that investors are focused on cost cuts and the spinoff.
insights.locator: Comcast also plans to split itself

insights.claim: The Wall Street Journal reports that Comcast's connectivity-and-platforms revenue fell 2.6 percent in constant currency in Q3 2026 to $19.66 billion, a steeper decline than Wall Street expected.
insights.speaker: The Wall Street Journal
insights.so_what: The core connectivity business is shrinking faster than consensus expected, a risk to estimates for the cable business that remains after the spinoff.

insights.claim: Comcast plans to split into two public companies by spinning off NBCUniversal and Sky. The plan was announced in June and is expected to close in mid-2027.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The mid-2027 spinoff is a catalyst; the cable business that remains will carry the broadband-erosion risk on its own.
insights.locator: Comcast also plans to split itself
